passage: I'm Sunaina, the project coordinator, and I've sat next to Nandini for a year. She fixes things that stall the rest of us for days. Last week the whole team was stuck on a memory leak in the billing system; Nandini found it in forty minutes, then apologised for "taking so long." When our manager suggested she lead the new module, she said, "Anyone here could do it, honestly, it's basic stuff." The next day I watched two senior engineers try the same kind of bug. They needed her help. At lunch she told me she still feels like she's bluffing. I don't know what she sees when she looks at her own work, but it isn't what the rest of us see.

qa.q: How long did Nandini take to find the memory leak?
qa.a: Nandini found it in forty minutes.

qa.q: Why does Nandini call the work basic stuff?
qa.a: Because the problems feel easy to her, she assumes they are easy for everyone, so her skill seems ordinary rather than rare, and she ends up doubting herself.

qa.q: How could Sunaina or the manager help Nandini see her skill more accurately?
qa.a: They could show her concrete comparisons, like how long the senior engineers took on the same bug, and ask her to lead the module with support.

qa.q: What is it like for Sunaina to hear Nandini say she feels like she's bluffing?
qa.a: Sunaina seems puzzled and a little sad, since the whole team relies on Nandini, who still cannot see her own ability.

grounding: Shows a skilled young woman engineer assuming what is easy for her is easy for all and doubting her ability, as seen by a colleague.

Monday: Gautam, the team manager, asked who could redesign the sensor code before the audit. Nikita stayed quiet. That evening she rewrote it anyway, "just to practise", and it ran twice as fast. She didn't mention it.
Thursday: Gautam found her file on the shared drive. "Did you do this?" "It's nothing," Nikita said. "Anyone could. It was obvious." He asked three others to try a similar task; none finished by evening.
Two weeks later: At the review, Gautam put her name on the slide. Nikita's ears went red. Afterwards she asked him, "Is it really that hard for others?" "Yes," he said. She sat with that for a long moment.

qa.a: It ran twice as fast.

qa.a: The task felt obvious to her, so she assumed it would be for anyone; her skill made the work seem easy and her own ability seem ordinary.

qa.q: What did Gautam do that helped, and what else could he do?

passage: Eshaan, you keep calling yourself average. Let your old Chinmay uncle tell you about Rukmini, who joined our bridge-design team the same year I did, long ago. She could look at a load drawing and spot the weak joint in minutes. The rest of us took hours. But she honestly believed everyone saw what she saw. At meetings she'd say, "This is probably obvious to all of you," and then explain something none of us had noticed. For years she turned down promotions, saying she wasn't ready. One day our chief showed her the review scores: hers were the best in the department. She laughed, sure it was a mistake. The best people I've known worried most about their gaps.

qa.q: How might the chief have felt when Rukmini laughed at her scores?

passage: The pumping station on the edge of Nashik lost power at two in the morning during the worst storm of the year. The backup pump wouldn't start, and water was rising in the basement. Rajni, twenty-four and the junior engineer on duty, traced the fault in twenty minutes by torchlight: a burnt relay and a wrongly set timer. She swapped the relay from a spare panel and reset the timer. The pump roared. When the supervisor, Vishal, arrived soaked at three, it was already done. "How did you find it so fast?" Rajni shrugged. "Anyone would have. It was just the relay." "Anyone? The last two engineers took a whole day with that panel." She shook her head. "They must have been busy." Later he asked her to lead the new training sessions. She said, "Maybe someone more senior?" Vishal frowned. "No. You."

qa.q: What was the fault Rajni found?
qa.a: A burnt relay and a wrongly set timer.

qa.q: Why does Rajni say "Anyone would have"?
qa.a: Rajni seems uncomfortable with praise, and because the fix felt easy to her, she assumes it would be easy for everyone. Her skill makes her notice how simple the problem was, not how rare her ability is.

qa.q: What choice could Rajni make when Vishal offers her the training sessions?
qa.a: She could accept and treat his evidence, the last two engineers taking a whole day, as a fair measure of her ability instead of her own doubts.

qa.q: How does Vishal see Rajni's work that night?
qa.a: He sees it as exceptional, since others struggled with the same panel for a day, and is frustrated that she doesn't see it herself.

grounding: A skilled young engineer fixes a pump fault fast during a storm but assumes anyone could have, and doubts she should lead training.

passage: The internal job post for senior design engineer at the Pune car-parts factory closed on Friday, and Indu hadn't applied. Her colleague Vaibhav found her at the canteen with a plate of misal. "You're the one who fixed the brake-bracket design in two days. The whole team was stuck for a month." "It was just a geometry thing," Indu said. "If you know the tool, it's obvious." "It wasn't obvious to me. Or to the senior people." She pushed the misal around. "Every time I learn something, I see ten more things I don't know. The guys who applied seem so sure." "Maybe that's because they see less," Vaibhav said. "You notice the gaps because you know the field." Indu was quiet. "You really think I should apply?" "I think you're the only one who's asking that question." She opened the job post on her phone before lunch ended.

qa.q: How long had the whole team been stuck on the brake-bracket design?
qa.a: The whole team was stuck for a month.

qa.q: Why does Indu feel less sure than the colleagues who applied?
qa.a: Indu feels insecure because each thing she learns shows her more she doesn't know. The easy fix felt obvious to her, so she didn't count it as special.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation with Vaibhav?
qa.a: When Vaibhav said Indu notices the gaps because she knows the field. That helped Indu see the doubt differently and open the job post.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel about Indu not applying?
qa.a: Vaibhav seems frustrated and wants Indu to be recognised, having seen her solve what the whole team couldn't.

grounding: A skilled young engineer thinks her fix was obvious and doubts herself, while less aware colleagues apply confidently.

passage: Deepak, you asked what my first year as an engineer was like. Mostly, I thought I was a fraud. I'm the only woman in our structural team, and every time I solved a load problem in ten minutes, I assumed it must be an easy one. Anyone could do it, I thought. When my senior asked me to explain it to the new hires, I apologised first: "Sorry, this is really basic." Then I watched three of them get stuck on the same beam for an hour. I still didn't believe it. I told myself they were tired. It took my manager showing me the review scores, mine at the top of the batch, for me to say out loud, "Manjula, maybe this is not easy. Maybe you're just good at it." Even saying it felt strange.

qa.q: How long did the new hires get stuck on the same beam?
qa.a: An hour.

qa.q: Why did Manjula feel like a fraud in the first year?
qa.a: Manjula felt doubtful and unsure, because the problems felt easy, so it seemed they must be easy for everyone.

qa.q: What could help Manjula judge her skill more accurately?
qa.a: Comparing the work with others' on the same task, like the new hires on the beam, and trusting records such as the review scores.

qa.q: How might the new hires feel when Manjula calls the problem basic?
qa.a: They might feel discouraged or small, struggling for an hour on something described as really basic.

grounding: A skilled young engineer recalls assuming her easy problems were easy for everyone and doubting her own ability.

passage: Nazia, you keep saying you're not good enough for the site lead role. Let Vasudha aunty tell you a story. When I was twenty-four, on the dam project, I could read a drawing and spot a mistake in seconds. I thought everyone could. passage: It was the week before the product launch, and the office in Aizawl was in chaos: the server kept crashing, and the lead engineer was sick. Lalremsiami, only two years into her job, quietly fixed the crash in an afternoon. She thought it was nothing. "Anyone could do it. It was just a memory leak." Mahima, the project manager, stared. What if they ask something I don't know?" That night she read three articles about memory leaks, sure she'd missed something obvious. She hadn't. passage: Rehana had been at the Hyderabad engineering firm for three years, and she was the one everyone came to when the design software broke. She fixed it in minutes, usually while eating lunch. passage:
I'm Rekha, and I build testing tools for a software company in Pune. For most of last year, I thought I was the weakest engineer on the team.

When I finished a task in two hours, I assumed it was an easy task. When others took two days on the same kind of thing, I thought they were being careful, and I was being sloppy. When my code had no bugs, I thought I'd been lucky.

Then Sangeeta, our lead, asked me to teach the new joiners how the test system works. I thought, why me? It's so basic.

In the first session, three of the five new joiners got lost in the first ten minutes. Something I found obvious, they had never even heard of.

Sangeeta said afterwards, "What's easy for you isn't easy for everyone. That's what skill looks like."

I'm still full of doubts. But I stopped calling my work basic.

qa.q: How many of the new joiners got lost in the first session?
qa.a: Three of the five new joiners got lost in the first ten minutes.

qa.q: Why did Rekha assume the tasks were easy?
qa.a: Rekha felt insecure and doubtful, assuming that anything easy for Rekha must be easy for everyone, so quick work seemed like luck or sloppiness.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta do that helped Rekha see the skill?
qa.a: Sangeeta gave Rekha a chance to teach, which showed the gap between Rekha and the new joiners, then named it as skill.

qa.q: How might the new joiners see Rekha after that session?
qa.a: The new joiners probably saw Rekha as an expert and felt a bit intimidated but grateful for the help.

grounding: A skilled young engineer assumes what comes easily is easy for all, and doubts that skill until teaching reveals it.

passage:
Team lead's note, structural design unit

Nikita joined eight months ago. Her calculations are the most accurate on the floor, and she finishes load checks in about half the time others take.

Yet in reviews she keeps saying things like "It was simple" or "Anyone could have done it." Last week, when I suggested she lead the bridge design review, she said she didn't think she was ready and that others "understood it better".

I've seen this before in strong young engineers. Because it comes easily to her, she assumes it's easy for everyone. She also sees every small gap in her knowledge, which the less experienced engineers don't even notice in theirs.

I shared with her, privately, the timing and error figures for the whole team. She was quiet for a long time, then said, "I didn't know."

She has agreed to co-lead the review with me. I'll keep giving her specific feedback until she believes it.

Avni

qa.q: How long ago did Nikita join the team?
qa.a: Nikita joined eight months ago.

qa.q: Why did Nikita say she wasn't ready to lead the review?
qa.a: Nikita felt doubtful and insecure, assuming her quick work was easy for everyone and noticing every small gap in her own knowledge.

qa.q: What did Avni do that helped Nikita see her own skill?
qa.a: Avni privately shared the team's timing and error figures, so Nikita saw real evidence of her ability.

qa.q: How might the other engineers see Nikita's work?
qa.a: The other engineers likely see Nikita as quick and reliable, and might be surprised she doubts herself.

grounding: A team lead notes a skilled young engineer who assumes her ease is everyone's and doubts her own ability.

passage:
Tuesday

Maria asked me again today how I fixed the pump control fault so fast. I said, "It was obvious, just look at the pressure readings." She looked at me like I was speaking another language.

I've been thinking about that look all evening.

I always assume that if I can do something, it must be easy. Everyone at the plant probably could, if they bothered. So when I fix something in an hour, I don't feel proud. I feel like I got an easy one.

But Maria has been here three years longer than me. And she didn't see it.

Maybe it's not obvious. Maybe I've just learned a lot without noticing. And maybe the reason I still feel unsure all the time is that I can see how much more there is to know.

Tomorrow I'm going to explain it to Maria step by step. Not "it's obvious". Actual steps.

Manjula

qa.q: What did Manjula fix so fast?
qa.a: The pump control fault.

qa.q: Why doesn't Manjula feel proud after fixing things quickly?
qa.a: Manjula feels unsure and doubtful, assuming anything Manjula can do must be easy, so a quick fix feels like getting an easy one.

qa.q: What plan does Manjula make for tomorrow, and why is it good?
qa.a: Manjula will explain the fix to Maria step by step, which respects Maria and helps Manjula see how much skill it really takes.

qa.q: How might Maria feel when Manjula says the fix was obvious?
qa.a: Maria may feel confused and a bit embarrassed, since it wasn't obvious to her despite her three extra years.

grounding: A skilled young engineer assumes fast fixes are easy for everyone, until a colleague's confusion shows otherwise.
